Constructing hierarchical helices for displaying nested temporal cycles in R

Richard Bischof

2025-03-04

In this vignette, I describe how to build and display hierarchical helices with a set of functions developed for this purpose. These functions are rudimentary; I wrote them to allow me explore the concept and to produce the figures in (Bischof 2025). Interested users are welcome to improve these functions or develop new ones.

First, we load the libraries and functions needed to run the examples.

library(rgl)
library(colorspace)
library(broman)
library(rgl)
library(suncalc)
library(R.utils)
library(worldmet)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)


sourceDirectory("FUNCTIONS", modifiedOnly=FALSE)

Basic (1\(^{st}\) order) helix

We can use function makeHelix to display the architecture of helices up to 3rd order. We start by constructing and plotting a simple helix (1\(^{st}\) order) with makeHelix. As arguments, we provide the number of helix loops we want displayed, as well as their radius. We also indicate the number of points we want each loop drawn with; more points make for a smoother appearance and slower calculations. Additional arguments allow further customization; we will accept their default values here.

hlx <- makeHelix(
  n.loops = 2 ,
  n.points = 20,
  radii = 3,
  plot = TRUE
)

You can use your cursor to move and rotate the three-dimensional constructs in this vignette and to zoom in and out. Instead of plotting directly with makeHelix, one can use the object (matrix) returned by the function to create customizable plots, e.g., with function plot3d in package rgl (Murdoch and Adler 2024).

2\(^{nd}\) order helix

We are now going to add a second helix that wraps around the first one. We provide a vector of radii (radius for the 1\(^{st}\) order helix, followed by the radius of the 2\(^{nd}\) order helix) and a vector with the number of loops. The latter indicates the number of loops we want to display for the 1st order helix and a second number that specifies the number of times we want the 2\(^{nd}\) order helix to wrap around each full loop of the 1\(^{st}\) order helix. In the example below, we give the 2\(^{nd}\) order helix a radius of 2 and wrap it 10 times around each full loop of the 1\(^{st}\) order helix. Argument n.points refers to the number of points we want to use to draw each loop, regardless of the order displayed.

hlx <- makeHelix(
  n.loops = c(4, 10),
  n.points = 20 ,
  radii = c(4, 2) ,
  plot = TRUE
)

3\(^{rd}\) order hierarchical helix

Function CalcHelix can construct hierarchical helices up to the 3\(^{rd}\) order. We add the 3\(^{rd}\) helix to the first two helices by extending the vector for argument radius with an additional radius (0.5) and the vector for argument n.loops with the number of times (20) we want the 3\(^{rd}\) order helix to wrap around each full loop of the 2\(^{nd}\) order helix.

hlx <- makeHelix(
  n.loops = c(4, 10, 20),
  n.points = 20,
  radii = c(4, 2, 0.5),
  plot = TRUE
)

Using helices to visualize temporal information

Function hHelix

The function hHelix configures and plots datetime data (using R’s POSIX class) as rendered helices. A version of this function was used to generate the plots in (Bischof 2025). A helix can be plotted using hHelix simply by providing the start and end date, as well as ordered vectors with the period (period, expressed in earth days) and radius (radii) of each loop. The entire helix will be composed of a sequence spheres, so we provide their radius (sphere.radius) as well. Increasing pts.per.hour will give the rendered helix a smoother appearance and allows information display at finer temporal resolution, but it will also increase computation/rendering time, especially for large temporal extents.

hHelix(
  sphere.radius = 0.12,
  pts.per.hour = 1,
  start = as.POSIXct("2020-01-01 06:00"),
  end = as.POSIXct("2020-01-06"),
  radii =  c(0.15),
  periods = c(eearth.day=1),
  )
## [1] "Creating helix"
## [1] "Adding Start Marker to Plot"

By default, a colored sphere is added to mark the start of the time series. This can be deactivated by setting mark.start = 0. The appearance of the rgl device and three-dimensional object (perspective, zoom, borders/axes, window size, etc.) can be controlled via functions such as view3d, box3d, bbox3d, and par3d in the rgl package.

We can wrap the day-helix around a lunar cycle helix, thereby creating a hierarchical helix of 2\(^{nd}\) order.

hHelix(
  sphere.radius = 0.08,
  pts.per.hour = 1,
  start = as.POSIXct("2020-01-01 06:00"),
  end = as.POSIXct("2020-03-01"),
  radii =  c(0.3, 0.15),
  periods = c(lunar.month=29.530575, earth.day=1),
  )
## [1] "Creating helix"
## [1] "Adding Start Marker to Plot"

Finally, we create a 3\(^{rd}\) order hierarchical helix for a 2-year period, with day loops wrapped around lunar loops wrapped around year loops.

hHelix(
  sphere.radius = 0.08,
  pts.per.hour = 1,
  start = as.POSIXct("2020-01-01 06:00"),
  end = as.POSIXct("2021-12-31"),
  radii =  c(1, 0.3, 0.15),
  periods = c(earth.year = 365.24237, lunar.month=29.530575, earth.day=1),
  )
## [1] "Creating helix"
## [1] "Adding Start Marker to Plot"

A meaningful display may require fiddling with the radii and sphere sizes, especially when changing the order of helices and periods.

Example 1: Displaying hourly air temperature values over the course of a year

Hierarchical helices created with function hHelix can be used to display temporal data in the context of nested regular cycles. The following example displays hourly air temperature values measure in Ås, Norway. The data are obtained using function importNOAA in package worldmet (Carslaw 2025) and are rendered in the shape of a hierarchical helix with cycles depicting earth days (24 hours) nested within lunar months (~29.5 days) nested within earth years (~365.24 days).

#---DOWNLOAD THE CLIMATE DATA FOR Ås, in Norway
dat <- worldmet::importNOAA(code = "014630-99999", year = 2015:2016)

periods <- c(earth.year = 365.24237,
             lunar.month = 29.530575,
             earth.day = 1)#---expressed in days


airtemp.dat <- dat %>% dplyr::select(date, air_temp) %>% rename(datetime =
                                                                  date)

#----USING ggplot TO CREATE COLOR SCALE
temp <- ggplot(airtemp.dat, mapping = aes(1:length(air_temp), air_temp)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = air_temp), size = 2) +
  scale_color_gradient2(
    low = "blue",
    mid = "white",
    high = "red",
    midpoint = 0
  )

g <- ggplot_build(temp)
airtemp.dat$col <- g$data[[1]]$colour


hHelix(
  skin.df = airtemp.dat,
  start = as.POSIXct("2015-01-01 06:00"),
  pts.per.hour = 1,
  sphere.radius = 0.08,
  size = as.numeric(difftime(
    max(airtemp.dat$datetime), min(airtemp.dat$datetime), units = "hours"
  )),
  radii = c(1, 0.3, 0.15),
  periods = periods,
  time.line = "00:00:00",
  time.line.color = "white"
  
)
## [1] "Creating helix"
## [1] "Adding time line to plot"
## [1] "Adding Start Marker to Plot"

Note that we can indicate the position of a given hour of the day (or multiple ones if a vector is provided) with the argument time.line. Above, I am displaying the position of midnight as a white line. We control the relative position of a given hour of the day along the loops by specifying the start time (or first time in skin.df). That time (06:00 am in the example), will be positioned along the outermost part of the day loops.

Example 2: Displaying solar and lunar illumination

As another example, we can render the same 3\(^{rd}\) helix with colors indicating astronomical lighting conditions (day/night, lunar illumination). These calculations are based on location and date-specific solar and lunar information obtainable, for example, with functions provided in package (Thieurmel and Elmarhraoui 2022).

lonlat <- c(longitude = 10.7925, latitude = 59.66604)#---COORDINATES FOR ÅS, NORWAY


light.dat <- tibble(datetime = seq(
  as.POSIXct("2020-01-01 00:00:00", tz = "Europe/Paris"),
  as.POSIXct("2020-05-31 00:00:00", tz = "Europe/Paris"),
  by = "hour"
)) %>% mutate(
  sun.altitude = getSunlightPosition(
    date = datetime,
    lat = lonlat[2],
    lon = lonlat[1],
    data = NULL,
    keep = c("altitude")
  )$altitude,
  moon.fraction = getMoonIllumination(date = datetime, keep = c("fraction"))$fraction
)


#----USING ggplot to GENERATE A COLOR SCALE ILLUMINATION DURING THE DAY (SUN ALTITUDE, AFTER SUNRISE) AND NIGHT (LUNAR PHASES, AFTER SUNSET)

temp <- ggplot(light.dat, mapping = aes(x = datetime, y = sun.altitude)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = sun.altitude), size = 2) +
  scale_color_gradient2(
    low = "red",
    mid = "yellow",
    high = "white",
    midpoint = 0
  )
g <- ggplot_build(temp)
light.dat$col <- g$data[[1]]$colour

temp <- ggplot(light.dat, mapping = aes(x = datetime, y = moon.fraction)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = moon.fraction), size = 2) +
  scale_color_gradient2(
    low = "black",
    mid = "black",
    high = "white",
    midpoint = 0
  )

g <- ggplot_build(temp)


light.dat$col <- ifelse(light.dat$sun.altitude <= -(0 * pi / 180),
                        g$data[[1]]$colour,
                        light.dat$col) #-(18 * pi/180)  to include twilight period


hHelix(
  skin.df = light.dat,
  start = as.POSIXct("2020-01-01 06:00", tz = "Europe/Paris"),
  pts.per.hour = 1,
  sphere.radius = 0.08,
  radii = c(1, 0.3, 0.15),
  periods = periods,
  time.line = "00:00:00",
  time.line.color = "white"
)
## [1] "Creating helix"
## [1] "Adding time line to plot"
## [1] "Adding Start Marker to Plot"

Example 3: Adding additional observations of timed events to the hierarchical helix

Additional timed events can be added to the helical structure. In the following example, we randomly sample 100 observations from the hourly sequence created above and add them as observations to the helix.

activity.dat <- tibble(datetime = sample(light.dat$datetime, 25),
                       col = sample(c("darkgreen", "brown"), 25, replace = TRUE))


hHelix(
  skin.df = light.dat,
  start = as.POSIXct("2020-01-01 06:00", tz = "Europe/Paris"),
  pts.per.hour = 1,
  marker.df = activity.dat,
  marker.radius = 0.085,
  marker.alpha = 0.75,
  sphere.radius = 0.08,
  radii = c(1, 0.3, 0.15),
  periods = periods,
  time.line = "00:00:00",
  time.line.color = "white"
)
## [1] "Creating helix"
## [1] "Adding timed markers to plot"
## [1] "Adding time line to plot"
## [1] "Adding Start Marker to Plot"
